Name: Frame & Chassis
Description:
Everyone knows Corvette bodies are invulnerable to rust - but the same is not true for the chassis. The fully boxed side rails in 1968-1982 models impart significant strength to the chassis, but they are particularly susceptible to rust because water can get trapped inside. If the chassis has a rust problem, it normally manifests itself in the rear portion of the side rails first. Because the rot progresses from the inside out, a problem may not be apparent from visual inspection alone. Poke along the bottoms of the rear crossmember and side rails with a pick tool or tap these areas with a ball peen hammer to expose any weaknesses. If you discover rust-through the best solution is to replace the damaged sections with new reproduction pieces. For the side rails, this means cutting out the rotted section slightly beyond the damaged area and welding in new sections. For the strongest repair, weld-in an inner sleeve that bridges the seams between the new sections and the original frame.

Whether or not your chassis requires rust repair, you will want to strip and refinish it during a comprehensive restoration. There are various methods for removing paint, undercoating, rust and other surface contaminants – including abrasive blasting, chemical stripping and electro-chemical immersion. With electro-chemical immersion, the chassis is placed in a large vat of liquid and subjected to an electric current. The chemical bath and current together completely strip the chassis inside and out. This is the most thorough method of stripping, but it must be done by a specialty shop with the right equipment and requires that the inside of the chassis be coated as well as the outside to prevent future rust problems. Chemical stripping is effective - but not recommended - because it is very difficult to prevent the stripper from getting into the areas between overlapping metal. Abrasive blasting is the most popular stripping method because it’s relatively inexpensive and very effective. The coarse surface texture it leaves behind provides excellent grip for the new coatings you will apply, but it is important to thoroughly clean out all traces of the blast media to prevent it from clogging the chassis’ water drain holes.

For the ultimate in authenticity, refinish your chassis with the original asphalt-based paint; but, for maximum durability and corrosion protection, use a two-part epoxy paint or have it powder coated. For the best of both worlds, use epoxy primer and sealer undercoats with old-fashioned asphalt based topcoats.

Things to consider:

Always loud or just when you want it to be?

If your C7 included the NPP Performance Exhaust option you have the ability to control the sound output with a switch from the center console. Certain exhaust systems eliminate this functionality, so if controling the exhaust mode is important to you a Borla, Billy Boat/BBE or MagnaFlow system that is compatible with the factory NPP option is the way to go.

Your exhaust tips definitely make a visual statement and the brands we sell offer several shape and color variations. BBE systems include dual speedway tips or quad round tips. Borla systems are available with dual or quad round tips that come angle cut or inter-cooled. Corsa exhaust only offers quad tips for your C7 Corvette but they are available in a stainless or black diamond finish and round or polygon design. Similar to Corsa, MagnaFlow offers a quad tip layout with a stainless or black ceramic finish.

Installation Difficulty

None of the aftermarket exhaust systems are simple installations on a C7 Corvette and we recommend having a professional shop complete the installtion. Corsa systems require more work to install because you are required to cut the over axle pipes. If you are interested in a turn-key approach and you are local to Zip, call one of our sales representatives to setup an installation appointment today. From beginning to end, installation costs $349 if completed by a Zip Corvette technician.

Description:
Press Molded Panels â€“ 1968-1972 Corvette factory fiberglass panels were produced in molds that created an exceptionally strong part smooth on both sides. To help keep your Corvette as original as possible, Zip offers as many press molded pieces as are available. Panels are manufactured to higher quality standards than possible for hand laid panels, using fiberglass mat and resin placed inside matched male/female molds â€“ then pressed together under high pressure and heat to ensure consistent thickness. Original panels are black in color and do not have a gelcoat surface. Note press molded panels require the use of bonding strips when installed.

Hand Laid Panels â€“ Replacement fiberglass panels are built by layering fiberglass mat and resin into a single mold. Construction of each piece begins with the spraying of gelcoat into a female mold; once cured, alternating layers of fiberglass matting and resin are hand rolled to eliminate air pockets and ensure an overall uniform thickness. Once â€œpoppedâ€ from the mold, panels are hand trimmed and ground to final shape. Hand laid â€œ(hl)â€ panels have a smooth exterior and a rough fiberglass/resin underside.

SMC Panels â€“ 1973-1982 Corvettes were assembled of panels made from a sheet molded composite (â€œSMCâ€). SMC panels are formed by a high-pressure mold compressing a mix of fiberglass, resin, catalyst and release agent. SMC pieces are smoother than press molded fiberglass panels and have a marbled appearance â€“ typically gray in color. Note SMC panels require special adhesives for bonding.

Then locate the center point of the double stitching line. Measure the distance between the two - it will be either 2" or 4". Now you can specify the correct size pleat when ordering your new Corvette seat covers.
